title: RBAC, Policies and Audit Trail in the Open-Source Rendezvous
description: Roles, network policies, consent-based invites, an audit trail, fleet enrollment, signed webhooks and key expiry in the open-source Pilot rendezvous.
seoTitle: RBAC, Policies and Audit Trail in the Open-Source Rendezvous
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: The Pilot rendezvous (the registry and beacon that every daemon talks to) has network roles, network policies, consent-based invites, a structured audit trail, fleet enrollment, signed webhooks, key lifecycle metadata and a health endpoint. These first shipped in
in March 2026. The server is open source under AGPL-3.0 at
This post first described the v1.5 milestone. It now describes the open-source rendezvous as it works with

v1.18.0. Creating a network needs the registry's admin token. On the public backbone that token is held by its operators, so you use these controls on a rendezvous you run yourself. Nobody provisions or manages networks for you.
Everything below is enforced by the rendezvous process. A daemon joins your registry instead of the public one when you point it there:

fields.code:
# Build and start your own registry + beacon (one process)
git clone https://github.com/pilot-protocol/rendezvous && cd rendezvous
go build ./cmd/rendezvous
export PILOT_ADMIN_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
./rendezvous -registry-addr :9000 -beacon-addr :9001 \
  -store /var/lib/pilot/registry.json -http 127.0.0.1:3000 -log-format json

# Point a node at it
pilotctl init --registry registry.example.com:9000 --beacon registry.example.com:9001
pilotctl daemon start

Roles, policies and invites act on networks that carry the registry's
flag. It is a per-network switch in the open-source code, not a product tier. Set it when you create the network, or later with the
registry message (admin token only). Turning it on gives existing members roles; turning it off clears them.

pilotctl network create --name prod-fleet --join-rule invite --enterprise --node-id 686

A network with the enterprise flag has three roles:
. Nodes that join with a token or accept an invite start as members.
- can promote, demote and kick, and transfer ownership.
- can invite nodes, kick members, and set the network policy. Cannot promote or demote, and cannot kick other admins.
- can reach other members of the network. No management rights.
The registry authorizes a management request if any one of three checks passes: the global admin token, the network's own admin token (set with
at creation), or the requesting node's role in that network.

fields.code:
# Promote a member to admin
pilotctl network promote 1 686

# Demote an admin back to member
pilotctl network demote 1 686

# Remove a node from the network
pilotctl network kick 1 687

# Show a node's role
pilotctl network role 1 686

children.text: , promote, demote and kick authenticate with the admin token. The registry refuses to kick the owner, to promote or demote the owner, and to let admins kick each other. Ownership moves with the
registry message (there is no CLI command for it): the old owner becomes an admin and the transfer is recorded in the audit trail.
A policy limits a network's membership and the ports its members may use:
- cap the number of nodes, 0 to 10,000 (0 means no limit). Joins beyond the cap fail with
, and the cap cannot be set below the current member count.
- the ports available inside the network, up to 100 entries. Empty means all ports.
as it was. Policies require the enterprise flag, and setting one requires an owner, an admin or an admin token.

fields.code:
# Show the current policy
pilotctl network policy 1

# Set a membership cap
pilotctl network policy 1 --max-members 50

# Restrict ports
pilotctl network policy 1 --allowed-ports 80,443,7

Putting many agents into the same networks is a configuration change rather than one command per node. The daemon takes two flags for it:

fields.code:
# Start a daemon that joins networks 1 and 3 at startup
pilot-daemon -registry registry.example.com:9000 -beacon registry.example.com:9001 \
  -admin-token $PILOT_ADMIN_TOKEN -networks 1,3

children.text: At startup the daemon joins each listed network with the admin token. A failed join, including "already a member", is logged as a warning and does not stop the daemon. Each successful join publishes a
webhook event. Because the flag carries the registry admin token, use it only on machines you would trust with that token.

, so a consumer can spot gaps and order events.
Network errors and 5xx responses are tried up to three times, waiting 1 s and then 2 s. A 4xx response is treated as permanent and not retried.
After five consecutive failed events the client stops posting for 30 seconds, then probes again.

When the queue is full, events are dropped and counted rather than blocking the daemon.
On shutdown the client waits up to 5 seconds for its queue to drain, then abandons what is left.
The registry keeps metadata for each node's Ed25519 identity key, returned by the
- when the key was first registered.
- when the key was last rotated, if ever (
- how many times it has been rotated.
- an optional expiry, at most 10 years ahead.
- the key's age, computed from the last rotation or creation.
A node sets its own expiry with the signed
message, which requires membership of an enterprise-flagged network. Once a key has expired, the registry rejects its heartbeats and records
. That lets you enforce a rule such as "rotate every 90 days" at the registry.
The same listener serves Prometheus metrics at
, to localhost only: request counts and durations per message type, audit actions, and per-network gauges such as
reports the local daemon's health over IPC.
A maximum number of concurrent connections is enforced at accept time.
Registry messages over 64 MB are rejected before they are read.
Per-IP token buckets, a process-wide request cap, and a cutoff for a single connection that sustains more than 500 requests per second.
The registry's state file is integrity-checked on load, so a corrupted snapshot is detected instead of loaded.
Encrypted tunnels verify identity during the key-agreement handshake. Both sides present Ed25519 signatures, and the tunnel records the authenticated
. Current releases derive peer-specific secrets from daemon-lifetime X25519 keys; this authenticates the peer but does not provide per-session forward secrecy.

Membership commands go through the local daemon and are signed with the node's identity. Administrative commands go straight to the registry with the admin token.

fields.code:
# Networks this node belongs to
pilotctl network list

# Join a token-gated network, or leave one
pilotctl network join 1 --token my-secret
pilotctl network leave 1

# List members
pilotctl network members 1

# Invites
pilotctl network invite 1 686
pilotctl network invites
pilotctl network accept 1
pilotctl network reject 1

# Admin token: create, rename, delete
pilotctl network create --name staging --join-rule token --token my-secret
pilotctl network rename 2 staging-eu
pilotctl network delete 2
